title: The Hawthorns — Albion, through the years
description: Explore The Hawthorns: Albion’s home since 1900. Discover the stands, archive photographs, memorials and matchdays that shaped the ground.

blocks.field4: One patch of the Black Country.
blocks.field5: A home for generations of Albion.
blocks.field11: A panoramic view of The Hawthorns under floodlights in December 2013

blocks.field3: Albion’s story began elsewhere. Stoney Lane had witnessed two FA Cup wins, but by the end of the nineteenth century the club needed a new ground.
blocks.field4: The new site stood beyond the town centre, on land associated with hawthorn bushes. It offered a fresh start. On 3 September 1900, The Hawthorns opened with a 1–1 draw against Derby County: Steve Bloomer scored the first goal, and Chippy Simmons replied for Albion.
blocks.field5: What followed was a continual process of building, adapting and returning. The stands changed; the name stayed.

blocks.field11: “The Brummie” carries one of the ground’s most familiar names. The former terracing was replaced as part of the move to an all-seater stadium, with the new stand completed in 1995.
blocks.field12: The ground’s earlier history includes a different kind of reuse: material from the old Handsworth Stand was moved to help cover the Birmingham Road terracing when the Rainbow Stand was built.
blocks.field15: The Halfords Lane side was rebuilt between 1979 and 1982. It later underwent a substantial refurbishment, reopening as the West Stand in 2008.
blocks.field16: That work included dressing rooms, dugouts, a tunnel, executive boxes and facilities for broadcasters: a reminder of how much of a ground’s life takes place behind its seats.
blocks.field19: The Rainbow Stand’s final match came on New Year’s Day 2001. Its replacement opened that August, with a league game against Grimsby Town.
blocks.field20: The new stand did much more than complete the enclosure around the pitch. It brought together offices, hospitality, the ticket office and club shop, changing how The Hawthorns worked throughout the week.
blocks.field23: The Smethwick End was the other major part of the 1995 redevelopment, as the old terrace gave way to seats.
blocks.field24: Together with the Birmingham Road End, it marked a change in how supporters experienced their home ground: familiar ends, reshaped for a new era of stadium design.

blocks.field3: In June 2025, Albion planted 20 hawthorn trees at the stadium. The hope was to welcome nesting song thrushes — bringing the bird and branch of the crest together at the ground again.
blocks.field5: Albion’s home is 551 feet above sea level.
blocks.field6: The club historian describes The Hawthorns as England’s highest league ground. An elevated setting for a Saturday afternoon.

blocks.field9: The club records that FA Cup crowd on 6 March 1937. It belongs to a very different stadium era from today’s seated ground.

blocks.field8: Jeff Astle’s memorial gates were unveiled on 11 July 2003. Their crowned number nine and cup-winning celebration make the entrance to the ground a place of remembrance as well as arrival.
blocks.field11: Tony Brown’s statue was unveiled in 2014. Albion’s record goalscorer and appearance maker has a permanent place near the ground, as well as in its record books.
